concepts.name: Cached tokens and input-token rate limits

questions.prompt: A model's next-token logits are divided by a temperature `t` before the softmax, and then top-p (nucleus) sampling with `p = 0.9` picks the token. What does each setting do?

choices.text: `t` sets how many tokens are kept; top-p then rescales the logits before softmax
Low `t` favours likely tokens; top-p samples the smallest set with 90% of mass
Low `t` favours rare tokens; top-p always keeps the 90 most likely next tokens
Both only change length; top-p ends the answer once 90% of `max_tokens` is used

questions.explanation: Dividing the logits by a temperature below 1 sharpens the softmax towards high-probability tokens and shrinks the tail. Nucleus sampling then keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least `p`, so the set is small when the model is confident and large when it isn't. Keeping a fixed number of tokens is top-k, not top-p.

sources.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
sources.claim: Temperature divides the logits before the softmax, and t in [0, 1) skews the distribution towards high-probability tokens and lowers the tail's mass; Nucleus (top-p) sampling samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is at least p, so the set's size changes with the shape of the distribution, unlike top-k's fixed k.

questions.prompt: Your support agent sends a 40,000-token cached system prompt and tool list on every call, plus a few hundred new tokens. For most current Claude models, which input tokens count toward the input-tokens-per-minute (ITPM) limit?

choices.text: All input tokens, cached or not, since ITPM counts the whole prompt
Only `cache_read_input_tokens`, since new tokens are billed apart
Input and output tokens together, in one tokens-per-minute pool
`input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`, not cache reads

questions.explanation: Claude's ITPM limit is cache-aware: uncached input (`input_tokens`) and tokens being written to the cache count, but tokens read from the cache don't, on most models. So a well-cached prompt raises your effective throughput: with 2,000,000 ITPM and an 80% hit rate you can process about 10,000,000 input tokens a minute. Output has its own OTPM limit.

sources.title: Rate limits
sources.claim: For most Claude models only uncached input tokens count toward ITPM: `input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens` count, `cache_read_input_tokens` do not; with a 2,000,000 ITPM limit and an 80% cache hit rate you could process 10,000,000 total input tokens per minute. Limits use a token bucket, and exceeding one returns a 429 with a `retry-after` header.

questions.prompt: You are chunking 100 pages of help-centre articles for RAG with a recursive text splitter. How do you choose the chunk size and overlap, and how do you check the choice?

model_answer.summary: Split on natural boundaries, size chunks so each holds one retrievable idea within the embedding model's limit, add a modest overlap so facts at a boundary survive, and pick the settings by measuring retrieval on your own queries.
key_points: A recursive splitter tries paragraph breaks, then line breaks, then spaces, so chunks keep related text together

Chunks that are too small or too large both hurt retrieval, and text past the embedding model's input limit may be truncated; `chunk_size` is in characters by default unless you pass a token `length_function`
Overlap repeats some text between neighbouring chunks so information split across a boundary isn't lost
Test a range of sizes on a representative set of queries you can score, and keep the best one, rather than guessing

questions.explanation: There is no universal chunk size: it depends on the content, the embedding model and the queries. The tempting answer is a fixed number from a tutorial, but the reliable one is to compare a few settings on queries from your own data and measure which retrieves the right chunks.

questions.prompt: Your team wants steadier output from an extraction step on Claude Opus 4.7 or later, and plans to lower `temperature` and `top_p`. Explain what each parameter does, and what you would do on these models instead.

model_answer.summary: Temperature reshapes the softmax and top-p truncates it to the most likely tokens, but Claude Opus 4.7 and later reject non-default sampling values, so you omit them and steer the output with prompting.
key_points: Temperature divides the logits before the softmax; a low value pushes probability towards the likeliest tokens, at the cost of diversity
Top-p samples from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least `p`, so the set's size adapts to the distribution
On Claude Opus 4.7 and later, a non-default `temperature`, `top_p` or `top_k` returns a 400 error
So remove the sampling parameters and guide the behaviour with the prompt instead

questions.explanation: Knowing what the knobs do still matters for other models and for interviews, but on recent Claude models the API refuses them. Code that keeps sending `temperature: 0` breaks on migration; Anthropic's guide says to omit the parameters and use prompting.

sources.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
sources.claim: Temperature divides the logits before the softmax, and t in [0, 1) skews the distribution towards high-probability tokens and lowers the tail's mass; Nucleus (top-p) sampling samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is at least p, so the set's size changes with the shape of the distribution, unlike top-k's fixed k.

sources.title: Migrating to Claude Opus 5.5
sources.claim: Setting `temperature`, `top_p` or `top_k` to any non-default value on Claude Opus 4.7 and later models returns a 400 error; the safest migration is to omit them and use prompting to guide the model's behaviour.

questions.prompt: Your organization has a 2,000,000 ITPM limit on a Claude model and an 80% prompt-cache hit rate. About how many total input tokens per minute can you process before ITPM stops you?

choices.text: About 2,000,000, since cached tokens count at their full size
About 10,000,000: 2M uncached plus 8M read from the cache
About 20,000,000, since cache reads count at a tenth of size
About 1,600,000, since cache writes take 20% of the limit

questions.explanation: On most Claude models, cache reads don't count toward ITPM at all, so only the 20% uncached share uses the limit: 2M uncached tokens allow about 8M more from the cache, 10M in total. Cache reads are billed at a fraction of the input price, but that is pricing, not the rate limit.

sources.title: Rate limits
sources.claim: For most Claude models only uncached input tokens count toward ITPM: `input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens` count, `cache_read_input_tokens` do not; with a 2,000,000 ITPM limit and an 80% cache hit rate you could process 10,000,000 total input tokens per minute. Limits use a token bucket, and exceeding one returns a 429 with a `retry-after` header.

questions.prompt: You create `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200)` with no other arguments. What is `chunk_size` measured in, and where does it try to split first?

choices.text: Tokens of the embedding model; it splits at sentence ends first
Words; it splits on spaces first, then on newlines if still too long

Characters; it tries blank lines (`

`), then `
`, then spaces
Bytes; it cuts at exactly 1,000 bytes, then steps back 200 bytes

questions.explanation: By default the splitter measures length in characters and tries its separators in order: blank lines, then newlines, then spaces, then single characters, so paragraphs stay whole when they fit. To size chunks in tokens you pass a token-counting `length_function`. The 200-character overlap repeats text between neighbouring chunks.

questions.prompt: You are chunking 100 pages of help-centre articles for RAG with LangChain's `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter`. Which of these statements about choosing `chunk_size` and `chunk_overlap` are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: `chunk_size` counts characters by default, unless you pass a token `length_function`
Overlap repeats some text between neighbouring chunks, so a fact cut at a split survives
One chunk size suits almost every corpus, so a tutorial's value needs no extra testing
The splitter tries sentence ends first, then falls back to paragraph and line breaks
Pick the size by scoring retrieval on representative queries over a range of sizes

questions.explanation: `chunk_size` is measured by `length_function`, which is `len` (characters) by default, so pass a tokenizer-based one if you think in tokens. `chunk_overlap` repeats text between neighbouring chunks so information split at a boundary isn't lost. There is no one-size-fits-all chunk size: test a range of sizes on your own data with queries you can score. The splitter goes from large units to small: paragraph breaks (`\n\n`) first, then line breaks, then spaces, not sentences first.

", " ", ""]` in that order, keeping paragraphs, then sentences, then words together; `chunk_size` is measured by `length_function`, which defaults to `len` (characters); `chunk_overlap` overlaps neighbouring chunks to reduce information lost when text is split.

sources.title: Chunking Strategies for LLM Applications
sources.claim: There is no one-size-fits-all chunking solution; choose the chunk size by testing a range of sizes on representative data and running queries whose quality you can evaluate, iteratively.

questions.prompt: Your team wants steadier output from an extraction step on Claude Opus 4.7 or later, and plans to lower `temperature` and `top_p`. Which of these statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Top-p keeps a fixed number of the likeliest tokens, and `p` sets that number
Temperature divides the logits before the softmax; low values favour likely tokens
On these models, a non-default `temperature` or `top_p` returns a 400 error
`temperature: 0` has always guaranteed identical output for identical requests
On these models, omit the sampling parameters and steer the output by prompting

questions.explanation: Temperature rescales the logits before the softmax, and a value below 1 shifts probability towards the likeliest tokens. On Claude Opus 4.7 and later, any non-default `temperature`, `top_p` or `top_k` is rejected with a 400 error, so Anthropic's advice is to omit them and guide the model with the prompt. Top-p doesn't keep a fixed number of tokens (that's top-k): it samples from the smallest set whose probabilities add up to at least `p`. And `temperature: 0` never guaranteed identical outputs, even on earlier models.

sources.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
sources.claim: With temperature t the softmax is computed over the logits divided by t, and t in [0, 1) skews the distribution towards high-probability tokens; nucleus (top-p) sampling draws from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is at least p, so the candidate pool expands and contracts, unlike a fixed top-k.

sources.title: Migrating to Claude Opus 5.5
sources.claim: Setting `temperature`, `top_p` or `top_k` to any non-default value on Claude Opus 4.7 and later returns a 400 error; the safest path is to omit them and use prompting to guide behaviour; `temperature = 0` never guaranteed identical outputs on prior models.
